content: Nineteen percent of tuberculosis (TB) cases are linked to undernutrition. Studies on TB prevalence among acutely malnourished children in high TB-burden areas reveal a wide range of prevalence, with 2–24% of these children being diagnosed with TB. However, a review of guidelines for managing acute malnutrition in high TB-burden countries shows that TB screening is not consistently included. Children and adolescents with TB often present with symptoms such as failure to thrive or weight loss, and severe malnutrition is a significant risk factor for TB in this population. Children receiving therapeutic nutritional treatment or supplementation but failing to gain weight or continuing to lose weight should be evaluated for chronic diseases like TB. Malnutrition can also lead to false-negative tuberculin skin tests (TST) due to its impact on the cell-mediated immune response. Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) increases the risk of rapid progression of TB disease. When using integrated treatment decision algorithms, children with SAM (defined as a weight-for-height Z-score of less than −3) should be assessed comprehensively, including scoring sections and diagnostic tools like chest X-rays (CXR) if available. Molecular diagnostic tests such as Xpert MTB/RIF or Ultra, or LF-LAM for children living with HIV, should be performed when available, and treatment should begin if the test is positive. Children with documented contact with a person with bacteriologically confirmed TB should also be started on TB treatment. Children with SAM who are started on TB treatment should receive a six-month treatment regimen (2HRZ(E)/4HR). They should not be treated with the shorter four-month regimen due to limited evidence in this subgroup, as shown in the SHINE trial. If drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) is suspected, second-line treatment regimens should be initiated, or the child should be referred to an appropriate level of care. Children and adolescents living with HIV and severe malnutrition who have TB are at high risk for poor treatment outcomes and mortality, necessitating close monitoring. Nutritional care is a critical component of TB management. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that all individuals with TB undergo nutritional assessment and receive appropriate counseling and support throughout their treatment. For children and adolescents with TB and SAM, management should align with WHO recommendations for SAM treatment. School-age children, adolescents, and adults with TB and moderate undernutrition who fail to regain normal body mass index after two months of TB treatment, or who lose weight during treatment, should be evaluated for adherence and comorbid conditions. They should also receive nutritional counseling and, if necessary, locally available nutrient-rich or fortified supplementary foods to restore normal nutritional status. In settings where contact tracing is implemented, household contacts of individuals with TB should undergo nutritional screening and assessment as part of the investigation. Nutritional support should be provided to children with TB who do not meet criteria for SAM treatment, including efforts to continue breastfeeding (up to 24 months if possible) and ensuring adequate nutrient intake through locally available and affordable foods. Additional energy intake (20–30% more calories) is particularly important during the intensive phase of TB treatment and can be provided through additional household foods as part of a balanced diet. Infants under six months of age with malnutrition or growth failure require referral to therapeutic feeding programs to receive specially formulated nutritional mixtures. If therapeutic feeding is unavailable, breastfeeding mothers should receive nutritional support to optimize breastfeeding. This warrants specific approaches to TB screening, preventive treatment, diagnosis, and management, with adaptations to avoid drug-drug interactions between antiretroviral therapy (ART) and TB medications. ART should be initiated as soon as possible within two weeks of starting TB treatment in children with TB/HIV coinfection. TB during pregnancy is associated with adverse maternal outcomes, complications during birth, and increased risks of preterm birth, low birth weight, and perinatal death. Pregnant women, particularly those living with HIV, should be prioritized for TB screening. Neonates born to mothers with TB disease should receive TB preventive treatment (TPT) and delay Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination until after completing TPT. Palliative care for children and adolescents with TB focuses on improving quality of life through symptom control, psychological support, and end-of-life care, including pain relief. TB services should be adapted to be more adolescent-friendly to address these challenges effectively. In children with pneumonia, TB should be considered as a potential cause or comorbidity, particularly in TB-endemic settings. Children with prolonged symptoms, treatment failure, or recurrent pneumonia should be evaluated for TB, and bacteriological confirmation should be sought whenever feasible. Post-discharge follow-up of children with severe pneumonia provides an opportunity to identify and treat coexisting TB. Undernutrition increases the risk of TB, and TB disease itself leads to weight loss and wasting. Children with SAM should be treated with a six-month TB treatment regimen. Nutritional assessment, counseling, and supplementation are recommended for children with TB who have moderate or severe malnutrition. Nutritional monitoring and support should begin early in TB treatment, particularly if nutritional indicators approach the threshold for severe undernutrition.
